newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindu party may lend Deve Gowda a hand.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindu party may lend Deve Gowda a hand.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda might win a helping hand in a vote of confidence next week from an unlikely ally, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), politicians said on Wednesday.
The main opposition party opposes Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front coalition.
But it could abstain in the trust vote set for April 11, ensuring victory for the prime minister, because it does not want to propel the Congress party into power, they said.
"The BJP is truly terrified of elections under a Congress government," a leader of the ruling United Front alliance told Reuters.

"Its assessment, a correct one I believe, is that the Congress would win over powerful regional satraps from the United Front as its own electoral allies. The BJP knows that would be disastrous for its own survival."

A senior BJP official said on Tuesday his party would prefer to face elections, which many analysts believe will come soon irrespective of the outcome of the test vote, under Deve Gowda rather than Congress president Sitaram Kesri.
"We would rather have Deve Gowda as interim prime minister than Kesri," a senior BJP leader said on Tuesday.
Kesri suprised friends and foes on Sunday when he announced that Congress had withdrawn its make-or-break support for Deve Gowda's 10-month-old centre-left coalition.

Congress leaders said Kesri's excellent ties with Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav, a former chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, could prompt the two to forge an alliance in India's most populous state.
Kesri's good standing with Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of the second most populous state of Bihar, was also at the back of the BJP's mind.

"If he gets both these state leaders, given their influence with Moslem voters and lower caste Hindus, it could have a powerful nationwide impact in favour of the Congress," one Kesri aide told Reuters.

Asked if the BJP could abstain in the test vote, a senior official in the rightwing party said: "We could. We can keep Deve Gowda as prime minister, until we decide to face elections under his government rather than Kesri's."
The BJP feared that if Deve Gowda lost the test vote, President Shankar Dayal Sharma could ask Kesri to form a new government.
"By abstaining for the confidence vote, the BJP could give Deve Gowda a new lease of life," political analyst Pran Chopra said in a television interview.
The BJP controls 193 deputies in the 545-member Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament. The Congress has the support of 140 and Deve Gowda's coalition commands 180 lawmakers.
The BJP held power for 12 days in May after inconclusive general elections but quit when it was unable to muster enough support to win a vote of confidence.

By Tuesday, Kesri appeared to have realised that his hopes of succeeding Deve Gowda had receded. "I am not against any member of the Steering Committee (of the United Front). My only complaint is against Deve Gowda," he said.
Kesri's statement came after the United Front and the Congress, its ally-turned-foe, started talks to defuse the crisis that has engulfed Deve Gowda's government.
